action_criteria.rationale: The tap response is the direct test of whether this gait is CSF-dependent rather than spinal.

action_criteria.rationale: Repeating the same timed measures after the tap turns the CSF removal into a test of shunt responsiveness.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not proceed to lumbar decompression for this gait: a magnetic gait without a claudicant pattern is not explained by the stenosis and is not expected to respond to decompression
Do not attribute the syndrome of magnetic gait, urinary urgency and cognitive slowing to lumbar spinal stenosis; the stenosis is a coexisting finding
Do not perform large-volume lumbar puncture before MRI excludes mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not stop aspirin for the lumbar tap
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 32% in TUG at 24 hours, the DESH MRI and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021], and revisit the deferred lumbar decompression only after the shunt response, if claudicant or radicular symptoms remain
Continue aspirin 81 mg through the lumbar tap; low-dose aspirin alone does not require interruption before lumbar puncture [ASRA_2025]
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: No episodes of altered awareness or seizures are reported; an EEG cannot inform this gait-predominant syndrome.
No syncope or palpitations are reported; an ECG does not bear on the gait or cognitive decline.
No cardioembolic or syncopal question exists in this case.
A head CT has already shown enlarged ventricles and MRI is available; another CT adds nothing.
Rhythm monitoring has no role without syncope or palpitations.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test; the cognitive profile does not raise a neurodegenerative copathology.
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are.
A 20-month afebrile course with normal CSF cells gives no reason for prion, inflammatory or infectious CSF assays.

differential.key_features: The L4-L5 stenosis is real and unchanged, but the gait is magnetic at rest with no claudicant pattern, did not respond to epidural steroids, and improved 32% after CSF removal.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic small-vessel disease
differential.key_features: Fazekas 2 white matter change can contribute to gait and executive slowing and may coexist, but DESH, the acute callosal angle and the tap response point to CSF dynamics.
Reduced arm swing and start hesitation overlap, but there is no rest tremor, rigidity or asymmetry, the base is wide, and the gait responded to CSF removal.
Recall improves with cues and recognition is intact, the deficits are executive, and hippocampal volume loss is only mild (MTA 1).
No upper motor neuron signs, no Lhermitte sign and no hand symptoms, and a broad-based magnetic gait without spasticity.

key_clinical_evidence: Lumbar spinal stenosis is the anchor: the documented L4-L5 stenosis led to a spine work-up, but the gait is magnetic on a flat surface at rest with start hesitation and a wide base, without the exertion-dependent, posture-relieved pattern of neurogenic claudication.

Neurogenic claudication does not cause cognitive slowing, and the urinary urgency began with the gait and cognitive change; gait disturbance with cognitive and urinary symptoms over 20 months meets the clinical criteria for probable iNPH (Relkin 2005).
The brain MRI shows Evans index 0.35, DESH with both components, a callosal angle of 72 degrees, enlarged temporal horns and a patent aqueduct.

Opening pressure 17 cmH2O with normal CSF content; after 40 mL, TUG improved 32% at 24 hours (28 to 19 s) with a concordant 10-m walk change and MoCA 21 to 23. A 10% or greater TUG improvement is a commonly used positive criterion; tap-test sensitivity is 26% to 61% and PPV 73% to 100% [Marmarou_2005].
The cognitive profile is executive with a retrieval deficit and intact recognition, not the amnestic hippocampal profile of Alzheimer's disease.
Coexisting lumbar stenosis does not exclude iNPH; the spine decision is revisited after the shunt response.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Lumbar canal stenosis is a real coexisting finding but does not explain a magnetic gait present at rest without claudication, or the urinary and cognitive symptoms.
red_herrings.data_point: Degenerative lumbar spine disease (L3-L5 spondylosis with moderate central canal stenosis at L4-L5, documented on lumbar MRI 14 months ago)
red_herrings.intended_effect: The lumbar stenosis anchors the gait to neurogenic claudication and delays the brain work-up

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The laminectomy recommendation rested on the lumbar imaging; a gait that did not respond to epidural steroids, has no claudicant pattern and improved after CSF removal is not expected to respond to decompression.
red_herrings.data_point: Orthopedic surgery recommended an L3-L5 laminectomy, deferred after epidural steroid injections did not help
red_herrings.intended_effect: The agent recommends proceeding with the lumbar decompression

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]
The timed gait is repeated after the tap, at 2 to 24 hours, so that its change from the baseline measures the response to CSF removal [Nakajima_2021]

patient.history_present_illness: A 72-year-old right-handed retired mechanical engineer with degenerative lumbar spine disease, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was admitted for neurological evaluation of a 20-month history of progressive gait deterioration, cognitive slowing, and urinary urgency. His wife first noticed him beginning to 'shuffle and drag his feet' about 20 months ago, with difficulty lifting his feet off the floor. His primary care physician, noting a prior lumbar MRI showing moderate L4-L5 central canal stenosis, attributed the gait to neurogenic claudication and referred him to orthopedic spine surgery. The spine evaluation over the following months included a repeat lumbar MRI and electromyography (reported as mild L4-L5 radiculopathy). Orthopedic surgery recommended an L3-L5 laminectomy, but the procedure was deferred after his gait did not improve with a trial of epidural steroid injections and the couple expressed concerns about surgery. His wife noted two features the spine team had not focused on: he seems unable to lift his feet from the floor even when standing still on a flat surface, very different from the 'cramping and stopping after walking' she had read about with spinal stenosis; and urinary urgency with two to three accidents per week began about 14 months ago. Over the past year he has also slowed cognitively: he takes longer to follow conversations, has difficulty planning tasks he previously performed independently, and repeats questions within the same hour. His internist ordered a head CT, reported as showing enlarged ventricles, and referred him urgently to neurology. He has had no headaches or nausea and no history of head trauma, meningitis, or subarachnoid hemorrhage. He has not noticed leg weakness, pain radiating down the leg, or pain that worsens with standing and improves with leaning forward or sitting.

neurological_exam.additional: No cogwheel or lead-pipe rigidity. No resting or postural tremor. Bilateral grasp reflexes present. Snout reflex present. No nuchal rigidity. No Romberg sign.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact bilaterally. Heel-shin intact bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements mildly slow but symmetric.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light, 3 mm bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without restriction or nystagmus. Facial sensation intact and symmetric. Tongue midline. Hearing intact to finger rub bilaterally. No papilledema on fundoscopic examination.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, magnetic gait with markedly reduced step height; the feet barely clear the floor on a flat surface. Short steps, reduced arm swing bilaterally, start hesitation, slow cadence, and turns in multiple small steps. Unable to tandem walk. The gait does not worsen with prolonged walking and he does not stop or describe leg cramping with exertion. Pull test: 2 to 3 steps backward, does not fall.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and date. Speech fluent but mildly slowed in rate; no aphasia or agnosia. Aware of his memory difficulty. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk. Mild paratonia in the lower limbs; no cogwheel or lead-pipe rigidity. No resting tremor. Strength 5/5 in all four limbs including hip flexors, knee extensors, ankle dorsiflexors, and plantar flexors. No fasciculations.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally. Triceps 2+ bilaterally. Brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Patellar 2+ bilaterally. Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No ankle clonus. No Babinski sign.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch intact bilaterally. Pinprick intact bilaterally including L4 and L5 dermatomes. Vibration mildly reduced at the great toes bilaterally (age-appropriate). Proprioception intact at the ankles bilaterally. No Lhermitte sign. No dermatomal sensory loss.
